'''Lester Randolph Ford Jr.''' (September 23, 1927 – February 26, 2017) was an American [[mathematician]] specializing in [[flow network|network flow]] problems. He was the son of mathematician [[Lester R. Ford|Lester R. Ford Sr.]]<ref>{{MacTutor Biography|title=Lester Randolph Ford|id=Ford}}</ref>

Ford's paper with [[D. R. Fulkerson]] on the [[maximum flow problem]] and the [[Ford–Fulkerson algorithm]] for solving it, published as a technical report in 1954 and in a journal in 1956, established the [[max-flow min-cut theorem]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ford | first1 = L. R. Jr.
 | last2 = Fulkerson | first2 = D. R.
 | mr = 0079251
 | journal = [[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]]
 | pages = 399–404
 | title = Maximal flow through a network
 | url = http://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/lans/readings/routing/ford-max_flow-1956.pdf
 | volume = 8
 | year = 1956
 | doi=10.4153/cjm-1956-045-5| s2cid = 16109790
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Gass | first1 = Saul I.
 | last2 = Assad | first2 = Arjang
 | contribution = 1954 Max-flow min-cut theorem
 | isbn = 978-1-4020-8112-5
 | page = 96
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | series = International series in operations research & management science
 | title = An annotated timeline of operations research: an informal history
 | volume = 75
 | year = 2005}}.</ref> In 1962 they published ''Flows in Networks'' with [[Princeton University Press]].<ref>{{cite book
 | author = L. R. Ford 
 |author2=D. R. Fulkerson
 | year = 1962
 | title = Flows in Networks
 | url = https://archive.org/details/flowsinnetworks0000ford
 | url-access = registration
 | publisher = [[Princeton University Press]]
|isbn=9780691079622
 }}</ref> According to the preface, it "included topics that were purely mathematically motivated, together with those that are strictly utilitarian in concept." In his review, [[S.W. Golomb]] wrote, "This book is an attractive, well-written account of a fairly new topic in pure and applied combinatorial analysis."<ref>[[Solomon Golomb]] {{mr|id=0159700}}</ref> As a topic of continued interest, a new edition was published in 2010 with a new foreword by [[Robert G. Bland]] and [[James B. Orlin]].<ref>Ford & Fulkerson (2010) paperback edition of ''Flows in Networks'' {{ISBN|978-0-691-14667-6}} {{mr|id=2729968}}</ref>

In 1956, Ford developed the [[Bellman–Ford algorithm]] for finding [[shortest path]]s in [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]] that have negative weights,<ref>{{cite book
 |authorlink=L. R. Ford, Jr. | last=Ford | first=Lester R. Jr. |title=Network Flow Theory |date=August 14, 1956 |series=Paper P-923 |publisher=RAND Corporation |location=Santa Monica, California |url=http://www.rand.org/pubs/papers/P923.html}}</ref> two years before [[Richard Bellman]] also published the algorithm.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Bellman | first = Richard | authorlink = Richard Bellman | mr = 0102435 | journal = Quarterly of Applied Mathematics | pages = 87–90 | title = On a routing problem | volume = 16 | year = 1958| doi = 10.1090/qam/102435 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

With [[Selmer M. Johnson]], he developed the [[Ford–Johnson algorithm]] for sorting, which is of theoretical interest in connection with the problem of doing [[comparison sort]] with the fewest comparisons. For 20 years, this algorithm required the minimum number of comparisons.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Mahmoud | first = Hosam M.
 | contribution = 12.3.1 The Ford–Johnson algorithm
 | contribution-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=kM5v2YqMVuoC&pg=PA286
 | isbn = 9781118031131
 | pages = 286–288
 | publisher = John Wiley & Sons
 | series = Wiley Series in Discrete Mathematics and Optimization
 | title = Sorting: A Distribution Theory
 | volume = 54
 | year = 2011}}</ref>

In 1963 along with his father Lester R. Ford, he published an innovative textbook on [[calculus]].<ref>Lester Ford Sr. & Jr. (1963) [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015000971625;view=1up;seq=9 Calculus], McGraw-Hill via [[HathiTrust]].</ref> For a given function ''f'' and point ''x'', they defined a ''frame'' as a [[rectangle]] containing (''x'', ''f''(''x'')) with sides parallel to the axes of the plane (page 9). Frames are then exploited to define [[continuous function]]s (page 10) and to describe [[integrable function]]s (page 148).

== Personal information ==
Lester was born in [[Houston, Texas]] on September 23, 1927. He learned to play [[piano]] and the [[flute]] as a young man, continuing to play piano as he got older. He was also a whistler, frequently heard whistling while he worked on math or for fun.<ref>https://www.noozhawk.com/lester_r-_ford_jr-_of_santa_barbara_1927_2017/#:~:text=He%20had%20a%20passion%20for,a%20charity%20of%20your%20choice</ref>. For higher education he considered [[Harvard University|Harvard]] and [[Oberlin Conservatory]], but chose the [[University of Chicago]] which provided him a scholarship. He earned his bachelor's degree in 1949 and a masters in 1950. Ford continued his studies at [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] where he earned a Ph.D. in mathematics in 1953.

Ford's employers included the [[U. S. Army]], [[University of North Carolina]] and [[RAND Corporation]]. The Defense Research Corporation of [[Goleta, California]] employed him for forty years as he kept pace with [[digital revolution]]. Ford married twice. With his first wife, Janet Johnson, he had nine children, including [[Fred Ford (programmer)|Fred Ford]], programmer of the ''[[Star Control]]'' Universe. His second wife was Naoma Gower.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.noozhawk.com/article/lester_r._ford_jr._of_santa_barbara_1927_2017|title=Lester R. Ford Jr. of Santa Barbara, 1927-2017|first=|last=|work=noozhawk.com|date=2 March 2017 |access-date=17 March 2019}}</ref>
